profile.reading: Per Element Critical's own site, this Austin, Texas facility sits at 8025 North Interstate Highway 35, Austin, Texas 78753, in Travis County. The operator's own dedicated Austin page describes a 62,300 square foot standalone colocation facility with 9.5 MW of total utility power and N+1 redundant design; that utility power figure describes power access rather than a certified critical-IT-load rating, so it is not recorded here as critical_it_mw. This standalone colocation facility sits on a 7-acre private campus, positioned outside all floodplains near Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, per the operator's own dedicated Austin page; since this registry tracks only one Element Critical row in Travis County and the operator's own site names only one Austin facility, these figures are applied with high confidence. Element Critical is a privately held colocation operator, rebranded from Central Colo in 2017, backed by an investor group including Mercuria, 26North, Arctos, and Safanad per Mercuria's own press materials, and describes itself as a data center infrastructure provider specializing in high-density power and advanced cooling for demanding workloads including AI and GPU infrastructure, offering colocation from individual cabinets to custom suites supporting deployments up to 50 megawatts across its current three-market portfolio (Austin, Houston, and Chicago). No founding date or year-opened figure specific to this Austin facility was located in sourcing reachable this session. Northeast Austin, along Interstate 35, has drawn a mix of enterprise and colocation development distinct from the Domain/North Austin corridor favored by some larger developments in the metro, and this facility's positioning outside floodplains near Austin-Bergstrom reflects a common site-selection priority among data center operators in the Austin market.

reading.body:
Element Critical's Austin campus occupies 62,300 square feet on a 7-acre private campus near Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, positioned outside floodplains. The operator's own site reports 9.5 MW of total utility power with N+1 redundant design, though this figure describes power access rather than a certified critical-IT-load rating. The facility is a standalone colocation operation designed to support individual cabinets through custom suites.

This campus does not appear in the state's published-capacity ranking. Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities of which only 18 publish megawatt figures totaling 468 MW; this campus publishes no critical-IT-load specification and ranks outside the top 18 by published capacity in the state. Element Critical describes its portfolio as serving high-density AI and GPU workloads across three markets, with individual facilities supporting deployments up to 50 MW, but no certified IT load for this Austin location has been disclosed.

Without a published critical-IT-load figure, the campus's actual capacity for AI work remains unknown. The 9.5 MW utility access, less overhead and redundancy, might support roughly 150-250 racks at typical colocation density, or 600-1,000 at dense AI training assumptions of 40-80 kW per rack, but this is structural capacity only and does not indicate current utilization or tenant composition. The facility qualifies as a colocation platform available for AI deployment rather than a published committed-capacity campus.
